number of doctors employed in hospitals (1933-1949)

linkages: Municipal implementation dates collected in the Danish National Archives linked to town-level outcomes from the DNBH publication Causes of Death
Town outcome data connected to the Danish Statistical Commune Data Archive for socio-economic controls at the municipal level (Bentzon, 1975)

Municipalities aggregated into medical subdistricts (urban and rural parts of medical districts) and medical districts, where treatment is dated by the first non-zero number of visiting nurses in the Medical Report

sample.universe: The 87 Danish towns (urban municipalities) of the period 1933-1949, plus all urban and rural medical subdistricts (43) and the medical districts outside Copenhagen (23) used in the complementary analyses
sample.unit_of_observation: town-year (main analysis); medical subdistrict-year and medical district-year (complementary analyses)
selection_rules: All 87 Danish towns 1933-1949 in the main analysis
All figures and tables exclude the medical districts of Aabenraa and Sonderborg because they merge in the period
Analysis limited to the years up to 1949 because the program changed significantly after the 1940s
Robustness samples exclude the five major towns (Copenhagen/Frederiksberg, Aarhus, Odense, Aalborg, Esbjerg), leaving 81 towns
Further robustness samples exclude all towns with infant wards, leaving 77 towns
Table 6 keeps only towns with non-missing tax information (77 towns; 71 and 68 in the restricted samples) and the years 1933-1947
Table 5 uses a balanced event-study sample of towns contributing at least 5 years both before and after treatment initiation (47 towns meet the criteria)
Table 7 uses all 43 medical subdistricts, and a restricted sample of 36 that excludes subdistricts with at least one infant ward town
sample.period: 1933-1949 (1933-1947 where socio-economic town controls are used)
sample.n_observations: Town data: 483 treated and 996 untreated town years, of which 1377 small-town years and 102 major-town years (Table 2, p. 490). Subdistrict data: 311 treated and 420 untreated subdistrict years (Table 3, p. 490).
sample.n_individuals: 87 towns (81 / 77 / 71 / 68 in restricted samples); 43 medical subdistricts (36 excluding subdistricts with infant ward towns)

construction_notes: Outcome: the infant survival rate is the number of infants per 1000 live births surviving the first year of life, used in log-transformed form because most towns are very small and often see zero infant deaths per year (footnote 2, p. 485).
Treatment timing: municipalities implementing before July 1 are assigned treated in the given year, those implementing after July 1 in the following year (p. 489).

Subdistricts and districts are assigned treated as soon as the medical report reports a non-zero number of nurses employed; the entire subdistrict counts as treated even if only some of its municipalities are covered (p. 489).

All town characteristics except the tax variables come from non-yearly sources (Census 1930, 1940, 1945; nine elections 1920-1945); a linear approximation is used to arrive at yearly data (footnote 18, p. 489; Appendix A.1).

Town regressions are weighted by the average number of live births per town; the Table 5 event study is weighted by the number of live births in town and year; subdistrict regressions are weighted by the subdistrict-year number of live births (by average district population in the medical district regressions).

Subdistrict mortality rates are per 1000 population and in logs; the acute enteritis death rate is computed per 1000 live births and those regressions are weighted by live births (footnote 26, p. 492).
Cause-specific mortality is not available by age group, so for acute enteritis all deaths are assumed to be in the 0-1 age group (Appendix A.2).
All figures and tables exclude the districts of Aabenraa and Sonderborg (footnote 7, p. 486).

Cost calculations assign 6900 DKK to a typical visiting nurse for 1937-1949 (6002 DKK in 1941), use 122 nurses in 1941, a 65-year average life expectancy, and Statistics Denmark's price calculator to convert to 2003 and 2010 DKK/USD (Section 6, Table 8).

claims.statement: Implementation of the Danish universal home visiting program increased the log infant survival rate in Danish towns (all towns, 1933-1949).

treatment.label: Treatment indicator (home visiting program implemented in the town)

register_source.value: Danish National Archives: records on the accreditation of and refund to municipal home visiting programs, 1937-1949 (historical archival source; no Statistics Denmark register)

definition.value: Indicator taking the value 1 for all periods after implementation of the 1937 universal home visiting program in the town and 0 otherwise. Municipalities that implemented the program before July 1 are assigned to be treated in the given year; those implementing after July 1 are treated in the following year.

timing.value: Town-year; switches on in the town's year of program initiation, roll-out 1937-1949

register_source.value: DNBH annual publication Causes of Death: number of live births and number of infant deaths (0-1 year) at the town level (historical publication; no Statistics Denmark register)

definition.value: Log of the infant first-year survival rate, i.e. of the number of infants per 1000 live births surviving the first year of life in the town-year. The survival rate is used in log-transformed form because most towns are very small and see very few births and often zero infant deaths per year.

units.value: log points of the infant survival rate per 1000 live births, per switch of the treatment indicator from 0 to 1 (the paper reads 0.005 as a 0.5% increase in infant survival)

magnitude.interpretation: While I find that that the program increased infant survival by roughly 0.5% in my full sample, I find an effect of 0.8% when excluding the major towns.

estimand.target_population: Danish towns that implemented the home visiting program (all towns), town-years weighted by the average number of live births per town
estimand.time_horizon: All years from program implementation onwards: the treatment indicator equals 1 for all periods after implementation (sample 1933-1949)
estimand.formal_query: E[ln(survival rate) | do(Treated=1)] - E[ln(survival rate) | do(Treated=0)] for treated Danish town-years

population.description: Danish towns (urban municipalities), town-year observations 1933-1949; all towns (87 towns)
population.ages: infants in their first year of life
subgroups_defined: five major towns (Copenhagen/Frederiksberg, Aarhus, Odense, Aalborg, Esbjerg) vs all other towns
towns with vs without infant wards
population.selection: All 87 Danish towns (urban municipalities); all figures and tables exclude the medical districts of Aabenraa and Sonderborg because they merge in the period.

identification.source_of_variation: Staggered timing of municipal implementation of the 1937 Danish Act on the Home Visiting Program across Danish towns, 1937-1949; the roll-out was shaped by a shortage and slow inflow of qualified nurses, the DNBH's lengthy accreditation process for nurses and municipal programs, and local preferences of key actors such as GPs and politicians.

key_assumptions.assumption: The timing of treatment initiation across municipalities is largely exogenous: it was driven by the shortage and slow inflow of qualified nurses, the DNBH's lengthy accreditation process and local preferences of key actors, not by local infant mortality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Narrative evidence on nurse-education constraints, the DNBH accreditation process and the optional character of the program; Fig. 3 and footnote 13 show that pre-treatment log infant survival hardly predicts the implementation year (R2 of 0.01 and 0.00); the DNBH did not target high-mortality regions.

implies_edges.from: Unobserved town-level determinants of infant survival

key_assumptions.assumption: No diverging trends: absent the program, infant survival in early- and late-implementing towns would have evolved in the same way (common/parallel trends), conditional on town and year fixed effects and town-specific linear time trends.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Town-specific linear time trends are added in column 2; the event study in Table 5 shows insignificant coefficients for the years preceding treatment initiation; Fig. 4 shows a jump in fitted lines around initiation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No parallel interventions or policies that vary in the same geographical and temporal pattern as the implementation of the home visiting program.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument that remaining confounders would have to follow the same geographical and timely pattern; other policies of the period (sulfa drugs and antibiotics, the 1946 prenatal care expansion, vaccine programs) were national, and only the school doctor program showed regional variation.

implies_edges.from: Other contemporaneous health interventions and policies

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the program does not affect infant survival before its implementation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5: the coefficients for the year dummies are insignificant in the years preceding treatment initiation; the effect emerges only after actual treatment initiation.

implies_edges.from: Home visiting program implementation (Treated_{s,t})
implies_edges.to: Log infant survival rate in pre-implementation years

threats_discussed: Parallel interventions and diverging trends
Pre-existing philanthropic initiatives, above all infant wards, concentrated in the five major towns
Pre-treatment infant mortality predicting early treatment initiation
Other medical advances and policies of the period: new drugs and vaccines (sulfa drugs and other antibiotics), improved access to prenatal care in 1946, the expansion of the school doctor program
Municipalities possibly shifting resources away from other policy areas when funding the program
robustness_checks: Town-specific linear time trends (column 2)
Excluding the five major towns and towns with infant wards (panels 2 and 3)
Controlling for infant ward initiation instead of restricting the sample (footnote 20)

Adding time-varying socio-economic town controls (Table 6)
Event study on the balanced sample (Table 5)
Subdistrict and medical district data, including placebo causes of death (Table 7, Online Appendix Table B.7)
Unweighted estimates (Online Appendix Table B.4)
unresolved_confounders: Possible reallocation of municipal resources away from other policy areas, which the author judges to be of minor importance but does not test

estimator.value: OLS (weighted least squares) difference-in-differences with town and year fixed effects

estimation.specification: Eq. (1): Y_{s,t} = alpha + beta * Treated_{s,t} + mu_s + delta_t + epsilon_{s,t}
estimation.clustering: Clustered standard errors at the town level
estimation.weights: Weighted by the average number of live births per town

source_table.value: Table 4, panel 'All towns', column (1)

mediators_claimed: Nurses' promotion of breastfeeding and proper infant nutrition
Nurses' timely referral of sick infants to GPs and other medical professionals

heterogeneity.dimension: Town size and pre-existing interventions (five major towns and infant ward towns vs the remaining towns)
heterogeneity.finding: The effect is stronger where the major towns are excluded: the paper reads roughly 0.5% in the full sample, 0.8% excluding the five major towns and 0.6% in the most restricted sample (Table 4), and attributes the full-sample attenuation to pre-existing initiatives in the heavily weighted major towns.

implies_edges.from: Unobserved town-level determinants of infant survival

key_assumptions.assumption: The timing of treatment initiation across municipalities is largely exogenous: it was driven by the shortage and slow inflow of qualified nurses, the DNBH's lengthy accreditation process and local preferences of key actors, not by local infant mortality.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Narrative evidence on nurse-education constraints, the DNBH accreditation process and the optional character of the program; Fig. 3 and footnote 13 show that pre-treatment log infant survival hardly predicts the implementation year (R2 of 0.01 and 0.00); the DNBH did not target high-mortality regions.

implies_edges.from: Unobserved town-level determinants of infant survival

key_assumptions.assumption: No diverging trends: absent the program, infant survival in early- and late-implementing towns would have evolved in the same way (common/parallel trends), conditional on town and year fixed effects and town-specific linear time trends.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Town-specific linear time trends are added in column 2; the event study in Table 5 shows insignificant coefficients for the years preceding treatment initiation; Fig. 4 shows a jump in fitted lines around initiation.

key_assumptions.assumption: No parallel interventions or policies that vary in the same geographical and temporal pattern as the implementation of the home visiting program.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument that remaining confounders would have to follow the same geographical and timely pattern; other policies of the period (sulfa drugs and antibiotics, the 1946 prenatal care expansion, vaccine programs) were national, and only the school doctor program showed regional variation.

implies_edges.from: Other contemporaneous health interventions and policies

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the program does not affect infant survival before its implementation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 5: the coefficients for the year dummies are insignificant in the years preceding treatment initiation; the effect emerges only after actual treatment initiation.
